blindSummary:
This state/province saw the country's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the July 2019 pride march in its capital, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the main cathedral. In the run-up, the area's most senior church figure had a proclamation read in every church across the state/province. The district surrounding the capital had been declared an "LGBT-free" zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while councillors of the national ruling party filed a motion to stop it.

The official protective response improved materially: at the fourth pride march (September 2024), around 300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the state/province's police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern - organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-district mobilisation infrastructure.

This position sits below the national average - slightly better than the holdout state/province, which lacked this one's demonstrable five-year improvement in official protection, but below the state/province surrounding the national capital, where the institutional machinery runs the other way.
